catalog_quote: In my PhD dissertation (Harjula 2004) I have analysed the tonal system of Ha as a pitch-accent system, and according to this analysis there are two types of accents, i.e. lexical and grammatical accents. On the lexical level this means that all the verbal roots fall into two tonal classes, one accented and the other accent-less. For the other word classes the place of the accent also has to be defined in the lexicon. The lexical accents are realised as H tones on the mora with which they are lexically connected, unless they are moved or removed because of the grammatical accents. The phonetic changes are not taken into account here. The lexical accents, together with the grammatical accents or the absence of the accent, define the grammatical forms of the verbs. new_statements.rule_in_words: Ha has no reported dynamic stress; prominence is a tonal (pitch-)accent. Verb roots are lexically accented or accent-less; for nouns and other classes the accent's position is lexically listed; grammatical (tense) accents fall on prefixes or the first/second stem syllable and may shift or delete lexical accents; every accent surfaces as a H tone on its mora. Supporting: Harjula 2006 p. 178 'the pitch accent is contrastive in Ha'; Bichwa 2018 p. 88 'Giha is a tone-accent language', accented vs unaccented stems, with an accent on the penult hopping back one syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic noun stems realise their accent on the class prefix; object prefixes attract the stem's lexical accent; index forms/connexive carry floating accents realised on the following word with augment lengthening; tone-neutralising verb forms delete the root accent (Harjula 2004: 96-100). Bichwa 2018: 88 reports 'Penultimate Back Hopping' of an accent off the penult.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical/grammatical accent realised tonally; statements concern words in isolation and in phrases (accent shift across word boundary with index forms). No statement about stress, intensity or phrase-final lengthening as stress; the full grammar (Harjula 2004, Koeppe) was not accessible and may add detail.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Ha of the Kigoma Region, Tanzania (Harjula's fieldwork 1997-2003 around Kasulu/Kibondo/Kigoma; Bichwa's 'Giha' = same language, glottocode haaa1252, ISO haq). Harjula notes several mutually intelligible dialects but does not restrict the accent analysis to one.

sources.note: p. 96: Ha tonal system analysed (in her 2004 dissertation/grammar) as a pitch accent system with lexical and grammatical accents; verbal roots are accented vs accent-less; for other word classes the place of the accent is defined in the lexicon; accents realised as H tones on the mora they are lexically linked to, unless moved/removed by grammatical accents. No mention of (dynamic) stress.
